name: Hassan Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Hassan, thanks for talking with me. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group that isn't tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything here is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run an electric rope shovel at the iron ore pit, the big one with the bucket the size of a garage, and I lead the loading crew on my shift. My day is lining up haul trucks, keeping the dig face clean, and talking to the drill and blast guys about what's coming next. I love a clean, fast load cycle, it's like a dance when it goes right. What wears me out is the night shifts and knowing we took a pay cut in the last downturn that never came back.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Rosa, my wife, works part-time at the town library, and we've got a ten-year-old and a fourteen-year-old. The mortgage is on a bungalow out by the old rail yard. We've got maybe two weeks of money in the bank at any time, which is normal around here, but it's not great.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You mentioned you use technology a lot. In what way?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I use an AI chat app every day, mostly to look up fault codes on the shovel or to help me study. I'm halfway through an online certificate in automation and control systems. The guys tease me, they call me the professor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, see, it's a tool, not a monster, and nothing changes for us. I'd tell the crew they can stop worrying about it at lunch. Online I'd maybe post that the hype was overblown, but the useful bits are still useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd be a little disappointed. I've been studying the automation side because I thought the change was coming and I wanted to be ready for it. If it stalls, my certificate is still worth something, but less than I hoped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Finish the certificate anyway, because the shovel's control systems are getting more digital whatever happens. I'd push at the union's technology committee for a pay step for people with the extra skills. And keep chipping at the credit card, maybe a hundred a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a little bit of anticlimax.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If it stalls, would you still push for the pay step?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Even more, because then the company has no excuse. They want digital skills, they should pay for them, and it's a way to get back some of that downturn cut. I've already got the numbers written up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Rosa think of all your studying?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She's proud, but she also says I'm never in the room even when I'm in the room. Last week I was reading about sensor calibration at our son's football match. I need to fix that, honestly.

S0.say: I'd say AI turned out to be a tool, not a monster, and tell the crew to stop worrying at lunch. Online I'd say the hype was overblown but the useful parts still matter.
S0.think: Privately I'd be a little disappointed, because I've been studying automation to get ahead of the change. My certificate would still have value, just less than I hoped.
S0.do: Finishes his automation certificate anyway and pushes the union's technology committee for a pay step for extra skills. Pays about a hundred a month off the credit card.
S0.feel: Calm, with a touch of anticlimax.
S0.quote: Last week I was reading about sensor calibration at our son's football match.
S0.fieldNote: Hassan is the rare worker who would be mildly disappointed if AI fizzled, since he has already bet on it. He links skills to pay through the union rather than going it alone. His partner's complaint about his absence was a candid moment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is manageable if we organise it right: the union gets a seat at the table and every operator gets a path into the new jobs. I'd say it at the technology committee and I'd post it in the miners' forum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm one of the people who comes out fine, maybe even better. The pit will need people who can run the shovel remotely and troubleshoot the sensors, and that's what I'm training for. My worry is everyone else on the crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the certificate faster, cutting my sleep if I have to, and apply for the first remote-operations or automation tech posting. I'd set up a study group at the union hall on Sundays and teach what I know. And I'd tell Rosa we keep the budget tight for a year until I'm sure of the new role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly uneasy for the crew, a bit excited for me, and guilty about being excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me more about the guilt.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When the crew talks about losing their jobs and I'm thinking, that's my chance, I feel like a traitor. My dad was a union man his whole life. So the study group is partly to make myself feel better, I'll admit that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach at the study group first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How to use the AI to read a fault log, honestly. Half the crew think it's cheating. I'd show them it's just a fast way to read a thick manual.

S1.say: I'd say it's manageable if the union gets a seat at the table and every operator gets a path into new jobs. I'd say it at the technology committee and post it on the miners' forum.
S1.think: I really think I'd come out fine, maybe better, because the pit will need remote operators and sensor troubleshooters. My worry is the rest of my crew.
S1.do: Speeds up his certificate and applies for the first remote-operations or automation posting. Runs a Sunday study group at the union hall teaching AI tools, and keeps the household budget tight for a year.
S1.feel: Uneasy for the crew, a bit excited for himself, and guilty about the excitement.
S1.quote: When the crew talks about losing their jobs and I'm thinking, that's my chance, I feel like a traitor.
S1.fieldNote: Steady change looks like an opening for Hassan, but his progressive, union upbringing makes him uneasy about benefiting. He plans to turn his own skill into a group effort through a study group. The gap between his private excitement and public solidarity was clear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need emergency rules now: notice periods, wage insurance, and a share of the savings going to the workers who are replaced. Two years is not a transition, it's a cliff. I'd say that loudly, and I'm normally the calm one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, two years scares me because even my plan doesn't hold. If the AI can troubleshoot the sensors and run the shovel itself, my certificate is worth maybe a year. And a year of work with two weeks of savings isn't a cushion, it's a countdown.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grab any automation contract going, even short ones, even three hours away, and bank all of it. I'd sell the boat-trailer and the motorbike straight away. And I'd be at every union meeting pushing for a fund paid out of the robot savings, because I'd need it like everyone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. My stomach drops just thinking about it, because I always thought being early would save me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the AI itself to find a way through?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Of course, I'd be asking it every night what jobs are left and where. That's the strange part, using the thing that's replacing you to look for a job. I'd do it anyway, I'm not proud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your fourteen-year-old?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd probably understand it better than me. I'd tell her to learn the things the machines can't own: looking after people, organising them. And I'd tell her that her dad tried to get ahead and it still wasn't enough, because she should know that's possible.

S2.say: I'd say we need emergency rules now: notice periods, wage insurance and a share of the savings for replaced workers. I'd call two years a cliff, not a transition, and say it loudly.
S2.think: I think even my plan fails in two years, because AI could troubleshoot the sensors and run the shovel itself. A year of work with two weeks of savings would be a countdown, not a cushion.
S2.do: Takes any automation contract going, even far away, and banks the money. Sells the boat-trailer and motorbike at once and pushes the union for a fund paid from robot savings.
S2.feel: Alarmed, with a sinking stomach, because being early no longer protects him.
S2.quote: A year of work with two weeks of savings isn't a cushion, it's a countdown.
S2.fieldNote: The two-year picture breaks Hassan's main strategy of getting ahead, and he says so frankly. His adaptability turns into scrambling for short contracts and selling assets. He would still use AI to job hunt, noting the irony without shame.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us a real chance if we start this year: retraining, a public jobs plan for mining towns, and union rights over how automation comes in. I'd want to be on whatever committee the company sets up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I get three or four good years running or supervising the automated fleet, and those years matter. I could pay the card off and actually have savings. But I know the end point is the same, so I'd want a second skill outside mining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the certificate this year and go for the remote-ops supervisor job. I'd save hard, maybe three hundred a month once the new pay comes in. And I'd look at a part-time course in teaching or training adults, because someone has to help towns like ours through this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan I believe in. That's a different feeling from the two-year one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why teaching?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the study group is the best thing I've done in years. Watching Gus, who's fifty-six, read his first fault log on his own was better than any load record. Maybe people will still want a person to teach them, even if the robot knows more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does Rosa fit into the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd keep the library job, which is steady, and she's better with money than me, so she'd run the savings. I'd promise to stop studying at football matches. Maybe I'd even keep that promise.

S3.say: I'd say five years is a real chance if we start now with retraining, a public jobs plan for mining towns and union rights over automation. I'd want a seat on any company committee about it.
S3.think: I think I'd get three or four good years running or supervising the automated fleet, enough to clear the card and save. The end point is the same, so I'd want a second skill outside mining.
S3.do: Finishes the certificate this year and applies for a remote-ops supervisor job. Saves around three hundred a month and starts a part-time course in teaching adults.
S3.feel: Anxious but holding a plan he believes in.
S3.quote: Watching Gus, who's fifty-six, read his first fault log on his own was better than any load record.
S3.fieldNote: With five years Hassan regains confidence and starts thinking beyond mining, towards teaching adults. The study group has clearly changed what he values. He plans the household finances around his wife's steadier job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have no excuse now: ten years is enough to retrain a whole town if the company and the government pay their share. I'd push for a regional transition fund, the kind they set up when coal closed elsewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think ten years plays to my strengths. I can ride the automation wave in the pit for a while, build savings, and move into training or a public job before the end. I'd be fifty-three, the kids would be grown, and I'd still have some working years to give.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the certificate, take the remote-ops role, and start the adult teaching qualification in year two or three. We'd aim to get three months saved by year three, which would be a first. And I'd keep running the Sunday study group, maybe get the union to pay for the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in the normal way. Like a long shift where you know the plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any part of the ten-year picture that bothers you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That it lets people relax. Ten years sounds long, so the company waits, the government waits, and the crew waits, then it's year eight and nobody's ready. I've seen that with the pension changes, everyone ignored the letters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And what about the end point itself, when it arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I don't know what work looks like when the machines can do almost everything. Maybe teaching people to live with it is the last job. I can't see further than that, and I'd rather say so than pretend.

S4.say: I'd say ten years leaves no excuse, because that's enough to retrain a whole town if company and government pay their share. I'd push for a regional transition fund like those set up when coal closed elsewhere.
S4.think: I think ten years plays to my strengths: I can ride the automation wave, build savings and move into training or public work. At fifty-three, with grown kids, I'd still have working years to give.
S4.do: Finishes the certificate, takes a remote-ops role and starts an adult teaching qualification in year two or three. Aims for three months' savings by year three and keeps running the Sunday study group.
S4.feel: Uneasy in an ordinary way, like a long shift with a clear plan.
S4.quote: Ten years sounds long, so the company waits, the government waits, and the crew waits, then it's year eight and nobody's ready.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years suits Hassan's strengths and his life stage. His main fear shifts from himself to everyone else delaying. He was honest that he can't picture work once machines do almost everything.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it beats even the people who prepared. What would help is wage insurance, so if your pay drops in a new job the government tops it up for a few years, and a fund paid by the companies that use the robots. And paid study time, because I've been studying at midnight for two years.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what the crew is like. These are people who've pulled each other out of bad situations. Whatever happens, I'd want us to go through it together, not one by one.

headlineQuote: I always thought being early would save me.
portrait: Hassan Alvarez is a 43-year-old shovel operator and crew lead at an iron ore pit, with a library-worker wife, two children, a mortgage and about two weeks of savings. He uses AI daily and is studying automation, so he would be slightly disappointed if AI stalled and quietly hopeful under steady change, though guilty about gaining while his crew loses. The two-year AGI picture alarms him because it beats even early movers, while five and ten years let him plan a path into remote operations and then adult teaching. He stays loyal to his union roots and keeps turning his own skills into a study group for others.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it would overtake even workers like him who prepared early.
whatWouldHelp: Wage insurance that tops up lower pay in a new job, a fund paid by companies using robots, and paid study time.
